title: Stochastic figures compare random outputs with exact statistics, so read means, spreads and sample sizes, not single curves
summary: Sample paths against an exact mean and standard deviation, Monte Carlo error against sample size, an ensemble of mixing models and a randomized sub-grid viscosity are all pictures of distributions. The reading rule is the same: compare a statistic with its exact value, and ask how many samples stand behind each point.

media.alt: Left: Ornstein-Uhlenbeck sample paths, theta 2, mu 0, sigma 1, 2000 paths. Faint blue paths decay from 3 towards 0 with growing scatter; the blue ensemble mean, a black exact-mean curve and a shaded exact plus-or-minus-one-standard-deviation band lie on top of one another, the band narrowing to about plus and minus 0.5 by t = 3. Right: probability densities at t = 0, 0.3, 0.7 and 3 as noisy spiky kernel estimates, with low dashed exact Gaussians.

source.caption: Ornstein-Uhlenbeck sample paths
source.note: Four stochastic-module figures. Several panels have visible problems (spiky density estimates, single-replicate error curves, blank axes in the mixing grid, variance resetting in the mixing figure). The page teaches how to read such figures and flags what a reader should ask, using textbook statistics only.

read_the_figure.question: Does the sampled ensemble reproduce the exact statistics (mean, variance, density) it is meant to, and how many samples does each point rest on?
read_the_figure.axes: OU figure: left, x is time t and y is X(t); right, x is X and y is probability density P(X, t) at four times. Variance-reduction figure: left, x is sample size N (log), y is RMSE of the estimate (log); right, bars of effective speed-up relative to plain Monte Carlo. Mixing figure: variance of the scalar against dimensionless time, mean against time, and histograms of the scalar phi at t = 0, 1 and 3 for three models. SGS figure: histograms of sub-grid viscosity for three spreads, viscosity against strain rate, near-backscatter probability against spread, and an energy spectrum against wavenumber.
look_at: OU: the ensemble mean (blue) on the exact mean (black), and the dashed blue band on the shaded exact band. The band should settle at the stationary value, about 0.5.

OU density: a kernel estimate of 2000 samples should look like a smooth bump; here the solid curves are spiky and the dashed exact curves are low and smooth, so the density panel is not a convincing comparison.
Variance reduction: the curves should fall along their reference slopes when averaged over replications; here each curve is jagged and not monotone.
Mixing: the variance curves against the dashed IEM theory line, the constant mean at 0.5, and whether the histograms change between times.
SGS: the width of each viscosity histogram against the vertical dashed deterministic mean, and the red and blue curves of the spectrum against the black DNS curve beyond the dotted cutoff.
read_the_figure.proves: If the ensemble mean, variance and density agree with exact formulas, the sampler and the integrator are implemented correctly for that process. Efficiency claims (speed-up factors) and model claims (backscatter, spectra) need replicated runs and a reference, and cannot be read from a single sweep.
if_wrong: Ensemble statistics off by an amount that does not shrink with more paths: a bias in the integrator or the noise.
A noisy, non-monotone error curve: each point is a single random realisation. Average over many independent replications before reading a slope.
A variance that jumps back up in a mixing run: re-initialisation or a plotting artefact, because pure mixing cannot create variance.
A kernel density estimate that is spiky: a bandwidth far too small for the sample count.
A heavy-tailed viscosity whose mean is far above its median: results depend on rare large values and need many samples.
must_check: Number of paths or replications per point, and the random seed policy.
Exact reference drawn for every compared statistic.
Error bars or replicate scatter on every efficiency or error-against-N curve.
Speed-up claims are tied to a stated cost model (evaluations or wall-clock).
as_drawn: OU (theta 2, mu 0, sigma 1, x0 about 3, N = 2000): exact mean 3 e^(-2t), which is about 1.1 at t = 0.5; exact standard deviation tends to sigma / sqrt(2 theta) = 0.5, as drawn at t = 3. The stationary density peaks at 1 / (0.5 sqrt(2 pi)) = 0.80, as the dashed curve does.

Variance reduction (estimate E[U^2] = 1/3): RMSE for standard Monte Carlo about 0.024, 0.014, 0.008, 0.020, 0.026, 0.008 at N = 50, 100, 200, 500, 1000, 2000, not monotone. Bars show speed-ups 1, 4, 20 and 40 for standard, antithetic, control-variate and Sobol. The title says 10 to 100 times for smooth integrands.

Mixing (N = 600): variance falls from 0.25 to about 6e-4 at t Omega = 1, then returns to 0.25 and falls again; the histograms at t = 1 and t = 3 look the same; the mean stays at 0.5; one column and the last panel in each row are blank.

SGS: the viscosity histograms are skewed with long tails, the near-backscatter probability rises from about 21 percent to about 83 percent as the log spread goes from 0.2 to 1.2, and the stochastic spectrum lies between the Smagorinsky and DNS curves beyond the cutoff.

terms.meaning: A mean-reverting random process: dX = theta (mu - X) dt + sigma dW. It has exact mean, variance and stationary density, which makes it the standard test for stochastic integrators.
The long-time density of the process; for OU it is Gaussian with variance sigma squared over 2 theta.
The root-mean-square error of an average of N independent samples falls like one over the square root of N.
Methods (antithetic pairs, control variates, quasi-random points) that reach a given error with fewer samples.
Closures for molecular mixing of a scalar in particle methods. IEM relaxes each particle towards the mean; the others mix particles with one another.
A closure in which the unresolved-scale viscosity is drawn from a distribution rather than set to its mean, intended to represent fluctuations and energy backscatter.
A smooth histogram built by placing a small bump at each sample; its bandwidth sets the smoothness.

remember: Mean of a stochastic simulation is a statistic with its own sampling error: sigma over square root of N.
A single Monte Carlo run is one random draw; a slope needs replicates.
IEM keeps the mean exactly and decays the variance as exp(-2 Omega t).
A log-normal variable has mean above median by exp(s^2 / 2) for log-standard deviation s.
Pure mixing cannot increase scalar variance.

understand.title: Three ways to say 'the sampler is right'
understand.text: Compare the mean with the exact mean, the spread with the exact spread, and the density with the exact density. The OU left panel does the first two well. The density panel fails the third for presentation reasons, not necessarily because the sampler is wrong: a kernel estimate with too small a bandwidth looks spiky.

understand.title: Why efficiency curves need replicates
understand.text: The error of one Monte Carlo estimate is itself random, with a spread of the same size as the error. The curves in the variance-reduction panel are single draws per point, so their ups and downs are noise. A speed-up factor read from them is not reliable.

understand.title: What a stochastic closure changes
understand.text: If the viscosity is drawn from a log-normal distribution, its mean can differ widely from its median, and large spreads produce rare large values. The model is then governed by the tail. The near-backscatter curve and the spectrum say what the modeller wants from it: energy returned to the resolved scales near the cutoff.

steps.title: Exact mean of the OU process
steps.note: With mu = 0 and x0 = 3, theta = 2 this is 3 e^(-2t): about 1.10 at t = 0.5.

steps.title: Exact variance and stationary value
steps.note: The standard deviation tends to 0.5, which is the half-width of the shaded band at t = 3.

steps.title: Peak of the stationary density
steps.note: This is the height of the low dashed curve at t = 3: far below the spikes in the kernel estimate.

steps.title: Monte Carlo error
steps.note: For the integrand U squared with U uniform on [0,1], plain Monte Carlo has RMSE 0.298 / sqrt(N): about 0.042 at N = 50 and 0.0067 at N = 2000, which is the scale of the plotted points.

steps.title: Antithetic pair
steps.note: Pairing U with 1 - U cancels the linear part of U squared. A pair costs two evaluations, so against plain Monte Carlo at equal cost the gain is (4/45)/2 divided by 1/180, which is 8.

steps.title: Control variate
steps.note: Subtract a correlated quantity with known mean. The correlation of U squared with U is rho^2 = 15/16 here, so the variance falls by a factor of 16 at the same sample count.

steps.title: IEM variance decay
steps.note: The mean is unchanged because the deviations average to zero. This is the dashed theory line in the mixing figure, which has slope -2 on its log axis.

steps.title: Mean of a log-normal viscosity
steps.note: For log10 of the viscosity with s = 0.6 the ratio is 2.6; for s = 2 it exceeds 4e4. This is why the histograms for larger spreads in the SGS figure have axes extending to 10 to 100 times the mean.

worked.title: Expected Monte Carlo error versus the plotted RMSE
worked.problem: For standard Monte Carlo on E[U^2] the exact per-sample variance is 4/45. Compute the expected RMSE at N = 50, 200 and 2000 and compare with the plotted blue points (about 0.024, 0.008, 0.008).

solution.text: Divide by the square root of N.

worked.answer: The plotted values are of the same order but scatter below and above these expected values, as a single random draw per point would; they cannot establish an N^(-1/2) slope. The reference line drawn at the top of the panel sets the slope only; it is well above the data.

analyze.q: The antithetic and control-variate bars read 4 and 20, while the variances above give 8 and 16 for this integrand. List what could explain the difference.
analyze.hint: Cost model, single replicate, different integrand or control variate.

analyze.q: The mixing figure's variance returns to 0.25 at t Omega = 1 and 2. What could produce that, and why can it not be physical mixing?
The near-backscatter probability rises with the spread of log Cs. Why does the mean viscosity stay close to the deterministic one while that probability grows?
analyze.hint: Spread changes the tails, not the centre.

evaluate.q: Which statistic would you want added to the OU density panel to decide whether the sampler or the density estimate is at fault?
evaluate.hint: The sample mean and variance at the same time, and a histogram at a coarser bin width.

evaluate.q: Is a single sweep of RMSE against N enough to claim a factor of 40 for quasi-random sampling?

create: Redraw the variance-reduction panel with 200 replications per N, median and 10 to 90 percent bands, and fitted slopes in the legend.
Design a test that separates a bias in an SDE integrator from sampling noise: which two quantities do you vary and what do you plot?

checks.q: Why does the OU band narrow to 0.5 rather than to zero?
checks.answer: Mean reversion shrinks deviations but the noise adds new ones; the balance is the stationary variance sigma squared over 2 theta, whose square root is 0.5.

checks.q: Plain Monte Carlo with per-sample standard deviation 0.3 and N = 900: what is the RMSE?
A Monte Carlo error curve rises between two sample sizes. Does that contradict 1/sqrt(N)?
checks.answer: No. A single run's error is random, so it can rise; only the expected error over replications must fall as 1/sqrt(N).

checks.q: A mixing model that raises scalar variance during a run: acceptable?
checks.answer: No: molecular mixing cannot increase variance, so it signals a bug or a plotting artefact.

checks.q: How would you verify an SDE integrator with the OU process?
checks.answer: Run many paths, compare sample mean and variance with the exact formulas at several times, include error bars, and refine the step to see the bias fall at the scheme's order.

provenance.notes: Standard theory only; every figure number was read from the plots or computed. Owner review: the OU density panel is spiky; the variance-reduction curves are single replicates and the bars (4, 20, 40) differ from exact values (8 and 16) for this integrand; the mixing figure's variance resets and its t = 1 and t = 3 histograms are identical, with blank panels; the SGS figure's 'near-backscatter' needs a definition since a log-normal viscosity is never negative.
